title: Guiding the Milky Way
caption: Laser guide stars and the Milky Way above Unit Telescope 4, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Four powerful laser beams leave Unit Telescope 4, or Yepun, at ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile's Atacama Desert. Behind them, the familiar band of the Milky Way stretches across the sky, almost appearing to follow the beams, and a faint green wash of airglow tints the sky.

The beams form the VLT's 4 Laser Guide Star Facility, part of a technology called adaptive optics. Turbulence in the atmosphere makes stars twinkle and blur. To undo that, a deformable mirror reshapes itself as often as 1000 times a second, guided by the turbulence astronomers measure by watching a bright star in the field of view.

When no suitable star is available, they make one. The lasers shine at a very particular orange-yellow color, a wavelength of 589 nm, which excites sodium atoms about 90 km up so they glow like a star. Airglow is light given off naturally by atoms and molecules in the atmosphere, visible only where skies are free of light pollution.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the faint green airglow and the Milky Way appear stronger than they would to someone standing there.
